title: Basis functions, OLS uniqueness, and weighted risk
summary: Make the linear-model assumptions explicit: linear in parameters, full-rank uniqueness, weighted empirical risk, and the bridge from noise to regularization.
objectives: Represent nonlinear inputs with a linear basis
Keep validation and test roles separate

sourceRefs.role: past-exam dual ridge and validation alignment

sections.title: Lecture core · Linear in parameters, not necessarily in x
sections.body: A basis model has $f_w(x)=w^\top\phi(x)$. The input transformation $\phi(x)$ can contain $x^2$, Gaussian bumps, or other nonlinear features; the model is still linear in the unknown weights $w$. This is why a linear model can represent nonlinear functions when the basis is rich enough.

math.explanation: The weights appear only as a linear combination. Nonlinearity in the features changes the hypothesis class without changing the least-squares algebra in the weights.
math.name: Linear-in-parameters basis model
math.purpose: Use it to separate nonlinear feature construction from the linear parameter optimization problem.

sections.title: Textbook depth · OLS normal equations and uniqueness
sections.body: For design matrix $\Phi$, the squared-loss stationary condition is $\Phi^\top\Phi\hat w=\Phi^\top y$. The familiar inverse formula requires $\Phi^\top\Phi$ to be invertible, equivalently full column rank. Without that condition, the data may identify fitted values but not one unique coefficient vector.

math.explanation: The inverse is not a decorative step: it encodes the full-column-rank assumption. If two basis columns are duplicates, multiple coefficient vectors can produce the same predictions.
math.name: OLS normal equations and uniqueness
math.purpose: Use it to state the full-column-rank condition before applying the inverse closed form.

sections.title: Textbook depth · Weighted empirical risk
sections.body: Give example $i$ a positive weight $a_i$ and define $A=\operatorname{diag}(a_1,\ldots,a_N)$. The weighted objective is $\frac{1}{2}(\Phi w-y)^\top A(\Phi w-y)$. Its normal equations become $\Phi^\top A\Phi\hat w=\Phi^\top Ay$. Positive weights preserve strict convexity when $\Phi$ already has full column rank because $A^{\frac{1}{2}}\Phi$ has the same null-space test.

math.explanation: Weighted least squares is ordinary least squares after scaling row $i$ by $sqrt{a_i}$. This interpretation is the cleanest way to reason about existence and uniqueness.

symbols.meaning: diagonal matrix of positive example weights

math.name: Weighted empirical-risk estimator
math.purpose: Use it when observations have unequal importance and verify that the weighted normal matrix is invertible.

sections.title: Bridge · Noise can induce a ridge penalty
sections.body: If an input is perturbed by zero-mean independent noise and the expected squared loss is taken over that noise, the extra variance term penalizes sensitivity to the weights. In a simple linear model this becomes an L2-like term. The bridge is useful intuition, but it does not mean every regularizer came from noise.

sections.title: Assessment habit · State the assumption before the formula
sections.body: When a question asks whether OLS is unique, do not answer from the existence of a closed-form expression alone. Write the rank or invertibility assumption, then give a counterexample if it is absent. When a question asks for a hyperparameter choice, say validation—not test.

examples.title: Counterexample: OLS need not be unique
steps: Let $\Phi=[[1,1],[2,2]]$ and $y=[1,2]^\top$. The columns are identical, so $\operatorname{rank}(\Phi)=1<2$.
Every vector $w$ satisfying $w_1+w_2=1$ gives the same fitted values $\Phi w=[1,2]^\top$.

Therefore the predictions are fixed for this sample, but the coefficient vector is not unique. A pseudoinverse selects the minimum-norm solution; it does not restore identifiability in the original parameterization.
examples.answer: The statement 'OLS always has a unique solution' is false unless the normal matrix is invertible.

examples.title: Derive weighted OLS
steps: Start from $J(w)=\frac12(\Phi w-y)^\top A(\Phi w-y)$ with symmetric diagonal $A$.
Differentiate: $\nabla J=\Phi^\top A(\Phi w-y)$, then set it to zero.
Solve $\Phi^\top A\Phi w=\Phi^\top Ay$. If $A$ is positive definite and $\Phi$ has full column rank, the weighted normal matrix is positive definite and invertible.
examples.answer: The weighted solution is $w_A=(\Phi^\top A\Phi)^{-1}\Phi^\top Ay$.

criticalQuestions.prompt: What exactly is unique in OLS?
criticalQuestions.angle: separate coefficient uniqueness from fitted-value uniqueness
criticalQuestions.modelAnswer: A unique coefficient vector needs full column rank. With rank deficiency, several coefficient vectors can give the same fitted values; the pseudoinverse chooses one convention.

criticalQuestions.prompt: Why is a positive-weight matrix safe for uniqueness?
criticalQuestions.modelAnswer: The weighted objective is ordinary least squares on $\mathrm{A}^{\frac{1}{2}}\Phi$. If A is positive definite, $\mathrm{A}^{\frac{1}{2}}$ is invertible and does not create a new null direction, so full column rank is preserved.
